paras: The expulsion of Black telephone workers from Madison County, North Carolina, took place on July 17, 1903, when armed white men ordered a camp of about fifty Black employees of the Southern Bell Telephone and Telegraph Company out of the Doggett section of the county and fired a volley of shots as they left. No one was reported killed or injured, and no report of arrests appears in the coverage. An Associated Press dispatch from Asheville carried the story to papers from Vermont to Alabama, and North Carolina Democratic papers used it to point out that the county was a Republican stronghold and the home of Senator Pritchard.

The workers were building the company's long-distance line through the Doggett section of Madison County, west of Asheville. Their tents had been pitched on a mountainside in a district that the dispatch described as having "a strong anti-negro feeling." The Raleigh News and Observer noted that the county returned an average Republican majority of one thousand and was the home of both Senator Pritchard and the Republican state chairman.

According to the Asheville dispatch of July 18, a "delegation of heavily armed" men, called "white men" in one version and "citizens" in others, came to the camp on July 17 and ordered the workers to leave the "country" (the "county" in some versions). The workers did not wait for a second order and started down the mountain at once. A volley of fifty or more shots followed, which the New-York Tribune said was fired "to hasten their departure" and the Savannah Morning News said was meant "to impress the unwritten law of the mountaineers that the negro is not desired as even a temporary resident." No version reports anyone struck by the shots.

No report of arrests, an investigation, or any action by the telephone company or state officials was found. Three days later a Raleigh correspondent of the Wilmington Semi-weekly Messenger wrote that there was "considerable amusement among the democrats" at the way "the Madison county republican" had driven out the fifty workers. The same letter quoted a Republican as saying no Black people were allowed in neighboring Mitchell County, and recalled that mountaineers there had once chased a Black band hired by congressional candidate Richmond Pearson out of the county.

The Associated Press dispatch, dated Asheville, July 18, appeared on July 19 in the New-York Tribune, the Savannah Morning News and the Richmond Times Dispatch. The Montgomery Advertiser ran a shortened version the same day under the headline "Negroes Driven From Town," and the Barre Daily Times in Vermont printed it on July 20. In the Carolinas it ran in the Raleigh News and Observer and the Wilmington Semi-weekly Messenger on July 21. Weeklies at Sumter, Clinton and Pickens reprinted it over the next two days.

Headlines presented the expulsion as mountain custom: the Tribune's read "Whites Drive Negroes Out" over "North Carolina Mountaineers Won't Have Them Around," the Sumter paper's "Negroes Not Wanted," and the Pickens paper's "Mountaineers Said Move." The News and Observer headed the dispatch "March, Say the Mountaineers" and said the workers "Tramp to the Tune of Bullets." A rewrite in the Keowee Courier of South Carolina described the district as one "where a negro in the abstract is hated with a venomous wrath." In Massachusetts, the Springfield Weekly Republican placed the event in the "South Carolina Mountains" in its headline, though its text said North Carolina, and printed it in the same column as a letter from William James on the "lynching epidemic."

In North Carolina the story became a partisan point. The News and Observer's editorial paragraph stressed the county's Republican majority and its ties to Senator Pritchard, and closed, "The New York Evening Post will please take notice." The Watauga Democrat reprinted that paragraph two days later, crediting the News and Observer. All the reports found came from white papers, and no Black-press account of the expulsion was found.

bases: An armed group ordered a camp of about fifty Black workers to leave the county and fired a volley as they went; no one was reported hurt (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Asheville
accounts.gist: Fifty Black Southern Bell workers camped in the Doggett section were ordered out by a delegation of heavily armed men and left at once, while a volley of fifty or more shots was fired.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondent
accounts.gist: Democrats in Raleigh were amused that Madison County Republicans had driven out the fifty workers; a Republican said no Black people were allowed in Mitchell County.

framing.detail: The AP dispatch reported the expulsion as the mountaineers' 'unwritten law' without comment; headlines read 'Whites Drive Negroes Out' and 'Mountaineers Said Move'.
The News and Observer used the event as a partisan jab at Republicans and the New York Evening Post rather than commenting on the violence itself.
The Raleigh letter described Democratic 'amusement' and recounted a similar Mitchell County incident with sympathy for the 'poor black musicians'.
Northern papers (Barre, Springfield) ran short versions; Springfield set it beside William James's letter on the 'lynching epidemic'.

conflicts.note: The Springfield headline contradicts its own text; North Carolina is supported by every dateline and text.
Likely a typesetting variant of the same dispatch; the meaning is not materially different.
